summary: Discusses implementation techniques for tunneling with IP protocol number 4 encapsulation, particularly with IP Security and other protocols. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: IP in IP tunneling lets a packet cross a network that could not carry it on its own. The sending router puts the whole original packet inside a new IP header, and the router at the far end takes that outer header off and forwards the original packet. This memo explains how the two headers are built, and how the router at the tunnel entrance reacts when something fails inside the tunnel.

questions: what is ip in ip tunneling
how does mtu discovery work in tunnels
how does ip in ip encapsulation work
how does a tunnel report errors to the sender
subtitle: Carrying one IP packet inside another so it can cross a network that could not take it.

tldr.problem: Two parts of the Internet can have different capabilities or policies, so a packet from one cannot cross the other on its own.
tldr.mechanism: IP in IP tunneling, which uses IP protocol number 4, puts the original IP header and payload inside a second, outer IP header. The outer header names the two tunnel endpoints, and the inner header keeps the original sender and recipient.
tldr.outcome: The original packet arrives at the far end of the tunnel unchanged. The memo gives the field by field rules for building the outer header and for reporting tunnel failures back to the sender with ICMP messages.

today: RFC 1853 is an Informational memo from October 1995, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo itself notes that an effort was under way in the IETF Mobile-IP Working Group to produce an appropriate proposed standard for this issue, so it describes a long-standing practice rather than a standard to implement.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IP in IP encapsulation, IP protocol number 4, has long been used to bridge parts of the Internet that have different capabilities or policies. This memo describes implementation techniques used for many years by the Amateur Packet Radio network for joining a large mobile network, and also by early implementations of IP Security protocols.

IP in IP differs from later tunneling techniques, such as protocol numbers 98, 94, 53 and 47, because it does not insert a special header of its own between the two IP headers. The original, unadorned IP header is kept and simply wrapped in another standard IP header. The information here applies principally to encapsulation of IP version 4; other IP versions are described in separate documents.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo describes a way to send a packet across a network that would not normally carry it. The packet keeps its own address information, and a second header carries it across.

sections.title: Encapsulation and the Outer Header
sections.content:
The technique is simple. An outer IP header is added before the original IP header, and between the two there may be other headers for the path, such as security headers specific to the tunnel configuration. The outer header's source and destination identify the endpoints of the tunnel, the two routers that carry the traffic. The inner header's source and destination identify the original sender and recipient. Each header chains to the next using IP protocol values, and the outer header uses 4 when the inner header is IP and no other tunnel headers are in use.

The outer header's fields are set by rules. Type of Service is copied from the inner header, or another value may be used between cooperating peers, so that a tunnel does not silently change the service level the user asked for; the memo calls this the transparency principle. The Identification field gets a new number for each outer header, because the encapsulated datagram may already have been fragmented and the tunnel may fragment it again, and the tunnel fragments are reassembled by the decapsulator rather than the final destination. The Reserved field is ignored and set to zero. The Don't Fragment flag is copied from the inner header, which lets the originator control the trade-off between performance and fragmentation. The More Fragments flag is set as required when fragmenting and is not copied, for the same reason a separate Identification is used.

Time To Live in the outer header takes the default value from the most recent Assigned Numbers document, so that a long tunnel that was not anticipated does not interrupt the flow of datagrams between the endpoints. The inner time to live is decremented once before encapsulation and is not affected by decapsulation. The outer Source is an IP address associated with the interface used to send the datagram, and the outer Destination is the address of the tunnel decapsulator. Options are not copied from the inner header, though new options for the path may be added. Timestamp, Loose Source Route, Strict Source Route and Record Route are deliberately hidden inside the tunnel, and tunnels are often built to overcome the inadequacies of those options.
sections.plainLanguage: Each field in the outer header is set in a fixed way. Some fields are copied from the original header, some get a fresh value, and the source and destination name the two ends of the tunnel.

sections.title: Tunnel Management and Soft State
sections.content:
One of the routers inside the tunnel may hit an error while processing a datagram and send an ICMP error back to the encapsulator, the router where the tunnel begins. ICMP only requires routers to return 8 bytes, 64 bits, of the datagram beyond the IP header, which is not enough to include the whole encapsulated header. So the encapsulator generally cannot pass an ICMP message from inside the tunnel straight back to the host that sent the datagram.

The way round this is to keep soft state about each tunnel. The memo says a router should maintain at least three things: whether the end of the tunnel is reachable, whether the tunnel is congested, and the maximum transmission unit of the tunnel. ICMP messages arriving from inside the tunnel update that state. When a later datagram would break the tunnel's state, for example because its size exceeds the tunnel's maximum transmission unit while the Don't Fragment flag is set, the router sends the matching ICMP error to the originator but also forwards the datagram into the tunnel. Forwarding the datagram anyway is what lets the router learn that the tunnel state has changed.

The result is that ICMP messages from the encapsulating router do not match one for one with errors inside the tunnel, but they do reflect the state of the network accurately. Most ICMP error messages are not relevant to a tunnel. Parameter problems in particular are likely to come from a misconfigured encapsulator and must not be reported to the originator.
sections.plainLanguage: Errors inside a tunnel cannot be passed straight back to the original sender, because the error message carries too little of the packet. So the router at the tunnel entrance keeps a record of the tunnel's health and sends its own error message based on that record.

sections.title: Tunnel MTU Discovery
sections.content:
When the originator sets the Don't Fragment bit and it is copied into the outer IP header, the proper maximum transmission unit of the tunnel is learned from ICMP Type 3 Code 4, Datagram Too Big, errors reported to the encapsulator. To support originating hosts that use this capability, all implementations must support Path MTU Discovery within their tunnels.

The method has a second benefit. Any fragmentation caused by the size of the encapsulation header is done only once, after encapsulation. This prevents a single datagram from being fragmented more than once, which improves the processing efficiency of the routers on the path and of the tunnel decapsulator.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel learns its size limit from the same kind of error message that ordinary IP uses. Working this way means the packet is split into fragments only one time.

sections.title: Congestion
sections.content: The tunnel's soft state collects signs of congestion, such as an ICMP Type 4 Source Quench in a datagram from the decapsulator, the router at the far end of the tunnel. When the encapsulator forwards another datagram into the tunnel, it is appropriate to send Source Quench messages to the originator as well.
sections.plainLanguage: When the tunnel is congested, the router at its entrance passes that on to the original sender with a Source Quench message, the same one an ordinary router sends.

sections.title: Routing Failures
sections.content:
Because the time to live is reset every time a datagram is encapsulated, a routing loop inside a tunnel is especially dangerous when the datagram arrives back at the encapsulator. If the IP source of the datagram matches any of the encapsulator's own interfaces, an implementation must not encapsulate it again; the datagram is forwarded normally instead.

ICMP Type 11 Time Exceeded messages report routing loops inside the tunnel. ICMP Type 3 Destination Unreachable messages report delivery failures to the decapsulator, and that soft state must be reported to the originator as Type 3 Code 0 Network Unreachable.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet that loops inside a tunnel must not be wrapped again when it comes back to the tunnel entrance. The entrance router sends the original sender a network-unreachable message instead.
